source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Montezuma's Revenge with a plain downscaled-image cell (no game knowledge): phase 1 solved level 1 in 57% of 100 runs after 1.2B frames and visited a mean of 35 rooms. Score was still rising linearly when stopped.
numbers: Phase 1 mean score 57,439 (CI 47,843-67,224), 100 runs, 1.2B frames. Level 1 solved after mean 640M frames, 10.8 h on one 22-CPU machine (runs that solved it). After robustification, mean 43,763.
limits: Restores emulator state (needs a resettable simulator). Phase 1 runs in a deterministic setting; robustification is a separate imitation step.
agent_relevance: Even a crude, domain-free state key plus an archive and 'return first' beat all prior intrinsic-motivation agents. For an LLM agent, a crude state key (hash of progress facts) may be enough to start.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Adding easy domain knowledge to the cell (room, level, keys, x-y) raised scores and cut the cost of solving level 1 by about 11 times. Cell design is the main moderator of Go-Explore.
numbers: Phase 1 with domain knowledge: mean 148,220 (CI 144,580-151,730), 50 runs, mean 9.1 levels solved, 238 rooms. Level 1 solved after mean 57.6M frames (0.9 h) vs 640M without. After robustification mean 666,474, best run over 18M. Pitfall: mean 59,494 (max 107,363) vs prior state of the art of 0 under stochastic testing.
limits: The domain-knowledge cell is hand made and game specific. Numbers are from the 2019 version; the Nature version reports different final numbers (see b05).
agent_relevance: The cell representation (what counts as 'the same state') is the main knob. For us this is the state-key design for an archive of partial solutions; a good key is worth an order of magnitude.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Robustification from one demonstration is unreliable; many demonstrations fix it. In 51 of 57 level-1-solving runs the best trajectory depended on a game bug, which had to be filtered out.
numbers: Single-demonstration Backward Algorithm succeeded in only 40% of attempts. With 10 demonstrations it worked robustly. 51 of 57 best trajectories exploited the 'treasure room curse' bug and were filtered.
limits: Specific to Atari and to the Backward Algorithm. The bug exploit is a lesson about a strong searcher finding exploits.
agent_relevance: A strong archive search finds exploits. It needs an independent check on the final answer (our code-checked verification guardrails). One good partial solution is not robust; keep several.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Archive update rule and selection weights. A cell's trajectory is replaced only if the new one scores higher, or is shorter at equal score. 'Times chosen' counters are reset on replacement; the 'times seen' counter is not. Newly found cells (low visit counts) are preferred because they sit near the frontier.
numbers: Domain-knowledge runs prefer cells in the highest level reached, which cut time spent exploiting the treasure room bug. The paper says a weighting heuristic beat uniform selection, but marks it 'data not shown'.
limits: The advantage of weighted over uniform cell selection is asserted, not shown with numbers in this version. No clean ablation of 'return' versus 'archive' alone.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete selection rule to test: prefer rarely-chosen, recently-discovered nodes. The missing ablation means we must run our own test of 'return to best partial' vs 'restart'.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore (Nature 590:580-586; arXiv 2004.12919 v6)
finding: Nature version: with domain-knowledge cells, robustified policies reach Montezuma's Revenge mean 1,731,645 and Pitfall mean 102,571. With the generic cell it beats the state of the art in all 11 focus games under sticky-action evaluation, and the exploration phase finds superhuman trajectories in all 55 Atari games.
numbers: Pitfall 102,571 (max possible 112,000). Montezuma 1,731,645 vs human world record about 1.2M. Exploration phase beats state-of-the-art scores in 83.6% of 55 games. Focus games: 50 exploration runs each, 5 robustification runs; domain-knowledge: 100 exploration, 10 robustification.
limits: Montezuma score depends on removing the default time limit. Authors did not robustify the other 44 games because they are already solved.
agent_relevance: The robust result is that the archive-plus-return principle generalizes beyond two games. The highest numbers need both domain knowledge and a very long compute budget.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2021) First return, then explore (Nature; arXiv 2004.12919 v6)
finding: Policy-based Go-Explore (learns how to return instead of restoring the emulator) still beats the state of the art, so the gain is not just from resetting the simulator. In the explore step it flipped a coin between random actions and sampling the policy.
numbers: Mean 97,728 on Montezuma's Revenge and 20,093 on Pitfall (domain-knowledge cells). Policy sampling found over 4x more cells than random actions on both games.
limits: Scores are well below the restore-based version (1.73M and 102,571). So restoring state still gives a large share of the gain.
agent_relevance: An agent that can only return by replaying actions is the policy-based case; one that can save and reload state is the restore case, which is far stronger. The scaffold should keep exact restorable partial states (text snapshots, code files).

source: Ecoffet et al. (2021) First return, then explore (Nature; arXiv 2004.12919 v6)
finding: Simulated robot pick-and-place with extremely sparse reward. The exploration phase found successful trajectories reliably while an intrinsic-motivation control found no reward at all.
numbers: Robustified policies succeeded in 99% of trials. 200 exploration runs (50 per shelf). The control with intrinsic reward discovered only a fraction of the cells and found no reward, although it ran 50 times more frames than the Go-Explore exploration phase.
limits: Simulation only. Cell representation taken from simulator internal state.
agent_relevance: This is a test against the rival theory (intrinsic motivation). More curiosity reward did not substitute for an archive.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: detachment and derailment hypotheses
finding: The authors explain their gains by two failure modes of intrinsic motivation: detachment (forgetting how to reach a frontier) and derailment (randomness while returning stops you reaching it). It is a hypothesis; the papers do not isolate each cause with an ablation.
numbers: No direct numbers for the mechanism. Related: Bootstrapped DQN scores only about 100 on Montezuma according to the related-work section.
quote: We hypothesize that detachment and derailment are
limits: Competing explanations not excluded: gains could come from exploiting determinism and restores, from the cell key, or from sheer compute. The post-exploration study (b20) isolates part of it.
agent_relevance: Treat 'detachment' as a testable claim for LLM search: does a restart-from-scratch loop lose partial progress? Test it directly.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019, arXiv v4) Go-Explore: related work on tree search and RRT
finding: Go-Explore is set against rival families: UCT-style planners restart planning at each action and can cycle between a few states; graph search has no truly 'closed' nodes because edges are found only by trying; RRT also keeps an archive but first samples a goal to reach.
numbers: Prior planners and agents scored 0 on Montezuma without human demonstrations or full determinism, per the paper. SOORL averaged about 200 points.
limits: Qualitative comparison by the authors, not a head-to-head test.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold's tree or archive of attempts is closest to this family. Nodes can never be fully closed, so budget caps are needed.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Agent57: Outperforming the Atari Human Benchmark
finding: A rival with no archive and no state restore: Agent57 (intrinsic novelty plus a bandit that picks among exploration and exploitation policies) beats the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, including the hard-exploration ones.
numbers: Capped mean human-normalized score 100.00; 57 of 57 games above human. Median 1933.49, mean 4766.25. NGU alone: capped mean 95.07, 51 games above human. R2D2 (bandit): capped mean 96.93.
limits: Trained at large scale, with a different evaluation protocol from Go-Explore, so scores are not directly comparable. Per-game Montezuma and Pitfall values not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Shows that adaptively choosing among exploration modes with a bandit (see the bandit subfield) is a real rival to an archive, and needs no state restore, but it needs training.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025, ICLR) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: Replace Go-Explore's hand heuristics with an LLM that picks which archived state to return to, which action to try, and whether a new state is worth archiving. On Game of 24 with GPT-4 it reached 100% success, faster than every baseline including depth-first search.
numbers: Game of 24, 100 test problems: IGE 100% within 150 operations, 70.8% faster than DFS (next best); significant at 150 operations (chi-square, p<0.05). GPT-4 naive 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83. Tree of Thoughts reported 74% in its own setting (not comparable).
limits: IGE picks from a list of valid options, not free math. Budgets are counted in environment operations, not LLM calls or tokens, so compute per step is higher for IGE.
agent_relevance: The nearest published test of our idea. Archive plus LLM-judged 'interesting' beat plain LLM loops at equal environment steps. LLM calls per step are not counted.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore, Table 2 ablation (Game of 24 / BabyAI-Text Put-Next-To / TextWorld Cooking Game)
finding: Ablation of the three LLM-driven parts. Which part matters depends on horizon: in the short Game of 24, diverse LLM action choice matters most; in the long-horizon BabyAI and TextWorld, state selection and archive filtering matter. Classic Go-Explore with a visitation-frequency heuristic is far below IGE.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 seeds, 150 steps): IGE 100; classic Go-Explore about 38 (CI +/-22); removing LLM action choice 68; removing all three LLM parts 61. BabyAI and TextWorld: 25 seeds each; random actions as in classic GE gave a drastic drop (TextWorld Cooking Game 0 in some ablations vs 92 for IGE). Row-to-value mapping in the PDF table is partly garbled, so Game of 24 values are the most reliable.
limits: Garbled table layout; 25 seeds is small; single prompt set.
agent_relevance: Our design: keep the archive, but let the model score 'is this partial worth keeping' and 'which to expand'. The pruning step is not optional in long tasks.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore, BabyAI-Text, TextWorld and archive size analysis
finding: IGE solved tasks in 250 environment steps that an RL-trained LM needed 1.5M steps for, and succeeded in long-horizon games where Reflexion did not help. LLM archive filtering kept the archive small.
numbers: BabyAI 'put next to': 36% gain over second best (chi-square p<0.05). TextWorld Cooking Game: IGE beat ReAct by 36 points. Coin Collector: IGE the only method to find the solution (all others completely failed). Without filtering the archive was about 5x to 8x larger; Table 4: BabyAI 203.5 vs 25.5 states, TextWorld 22.4 vs 4.4 states (95% CI).
quote: Reflexion does not improve over ReAct in all the games we tested
limits: Reflexion omitted for BabyAI due to cost. 25 seeds per game. The authors' explanation for Reflexion's failure (history too long) was not tested.
agent_relevance: A direct counterpoint to 'just retry with a reflection'. Archived real states controlled context length better than an accumulating reflection log.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore, Table 3 (model choice) and prompt robustness
finding: The gain from the archive loop holds across base models and is largest for weaker ones; the margin over the best baseline shrinks with a strong self-reflecting model.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 seeds): GPT-4: naive 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83, IGE 100. Llama-3 400B: naive 44, ReAct 68, Reflexion 54, IGE 98. Claude Sonnet 3.5: naive 24, ReAct 58, Reflexion 80, IGE 86. With domain-general prompts IGE scored 96 vs 100 with tuned prompts.
limits: On Claude Sonnet 3.5 the IGE vs Reflexion gap (86 vs 80) was not significant. Only one task family used for the model comparison.
agent_relevance: The scaffold helps weak and strong models, but a strong self-reflecting model closes much of the gap. Expect a smaller effect on our best model; measure it.

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026, ICLR) Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
finding: An archive of coding agents with parent sampling from the whole archive beats keeping only the latest agent, and beats always expanding the best. This is the cleanest published 'archive vs no archive' ablation for LLM agents found so far.
numbers: SWE-bench / Polyglot: DGM 50.0% / 38.0%. Without open-ended exploration (no archive, keep latest) 23.0% / 14.0%. Without self-improvement 39.0% / 28.0%. DGM Greedy (always branch from the best) 39.7% / 30.0%. Start 20.0% / 14.0%. After 80 iterations.
limits: Table shows no confidence intervals and apparently a single run per setting. Small task subsets in the search stage. Expensive runs, so few repeats.
agent_relevance: Strong support for keeping all partials as stepping stones with non-zero selection probability, not only the best. Greedy return-to-best lost about 10 points.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Darwin Godel Machine, escape from dips and transfer
finding: The archive let the search pass through temporary score drops. Agents evolved on one benchmark transfer to the other benchmark, so gains are not only overfit.
numbers: At iterations 4 and 56 a child scored below its parent but its line later produced a new best. Best SWE-bench agent scored 28.9% on Polyglot (initial 14.2%). Best Polyglot agent scored 24.5% on SWE-bench (initial 20.0%).
limits: Transfer gains are smaller than in-domain gains. The self-modification setting differs from solving a single problem.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule that a lower-scoring partial can still be expanded; an early score is a noisy guide to future value.

source: Galloudec, Dellandrea (2023) Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore
finding: Cell design is fragile. Learned latent states with density-based goal sampling replace cells. LGE slightly outperforms Go-Explore (with a naive grid cell) on Pitfall and Montezuma, and clearly beats it in a maze and a robotic task. A poor cell can make Go-Explore fail entirely.
numbers: Metric is interquartile mean with 95% CI. In Atari LGE reached only about 5k cells on Montezuma, far fewer than full Go-Explore with domain knowledge and reset. The authors say including the key in the cell raises exploration by several orders of magnitude.
limits: Atari comparison is against Go-Explore with a simplified cell, not its best configuration. Per-game counts are in figures only.
agent_relevance: Shows what happens when hand-built cells are dropped: a lot is lost against the best hand-built one. If our state key omits a key fact, search can stall.

source: Galloudec, Dellandrea (2023) Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore, ablation and rivals
finding: Three ablations in the maze each hurt: no exploration after reaching the goal, uniform instead of low-density goal sampling, and no subgoal trajectory. Intrinsic curiosity, Skew-Fit and DIAYN did not beat random exploration in the maze.
numbers: All three ablations had a 'significant impact' (maze, figure only). Only LGE and Go-Explore significantly outperformed random exploration in the maze.
limits: The maze is simple. Effects are shown as curves with IQM and CI, no table of numbers.
agent_relevance: The 'explore after arrival' step and the 'choose rarely visited frontier' step both carry weight, which matches a go/explore split in the schema.

source: Hoeftmann, Robine, Harmeling (2022/2023) Time-Myopic Go-Explore (NeurIPS 2022 Deep RL Workshop)
finding: A learned time-distance state key keeps the archive far smaller than the original downscaled-image cells while matching or beating native Go-Explore on Gravitar at 1M frames. Native archives bloat with near-duplicate cells.
numbers: Mean over 20 runs. Gravitar archive after 1M frames: native 7,376 cells vs 381 entries for time-myopic, with a higher score. Montezuma: the native archive size explodes after score 400. Authors claim state of the art for Gravitar at 1M frames. Table 2 rows are garbled in the PDF, so per-game scores are not recorded here.
limits: Workshop paper. Native Go-Explore was run for only 1M frames, far below the original 1.2B. Per-game scores uncertain from the PDF layout.
agent_relevance: Archive size control matters: near-duplicate states slow selection. IGE's filtering result points the same way, from an independent route.

source: Yang, Moerland, Preuss, Plaat (2022) When to Go, and When to Explore: The Benefit of Post-Exploration in Intrinsic Motivation
finding: First clean on/off test of the 'explore after return' step inside one algorithm. Post-exploration beat no post-exploration on all three MiniGrid tasks, and its effect was larger than tuning exploration noise during goal reaching.
numbers: FourRooms, LavaCrossing, LavaGap (10 environment seeds on the last two). Fixed post-explore length 20 steps and proportional 0.8 of goal-reaching length were best and on par. Selective post-exploration (decay 0.01 or 0.05) slightly beat always post-exploring; fast decay (1.0) clearly hurt.
quote: post-exploration has a much stronger effect on performance than the amount of exploration during goal reaching
limits: Tabular, small MiniGrid mazes. Policy-based (not restore) variant. Workshop paper; effects shown in curves.
agent_relevance: Supports the 'return, then explore' split. Gives a tunable: how many steps to expand from a returned state, possibly adaptive on novelty.

source: Yang et al. (2022) Post-exploration, continuing-task control and over-pruning
finding: In a non-episodic setting where the agent simply sets a next goal from its current state, post-exploration still helps, so the gain is not just 'more steps after reaching the goal'. Over-aggressive decay of post-exploration stops learning.
numbers: Effect is less pronounced than in the episodic setting. Decay 1.0 makes the learning curve nearly flat near the end because the agent stops post-exploring. Hindsight relabelling of 50% of the trajectory used.
limits: Random post-exploration only; smarter post-exploration is untested. Not a replication of the Atari numbers.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: pruning how much we expand from archived states too hard stalls progress.

source: Koren, Kochenderfer (2020) Adaptive Stress Testing without Domain Heuristics using Go-Explore
finding: Go-Explore as a failure finder in a driving simulation with no heuristic reward. It finds failures that deep RL and MCTS cannot in the long-horizon case, but is worse than MCTS at short horizons and worse than deep RL when a heuristic reward exists.
numbers: Three scenarios. Easy with heuristic: all three find failures, Go-Explore worst, deep RL best. Medium, no heuristic: deep RL found no failure in 100 iterations; MCTS beat Go-Explore. Hard (longer horizon): only Go-Explore found failures; DRL and MCTS found none. A backward-algorithm robustification phase improved all three solvers.
limits: One simulated scenario family, 100 iterations, no repeated-seed statistics shown. Domain specific.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: archives win on long horizons without a dense signal and lose to simpler search on short horizons. Choose by horizon length.

source: Bhatt, Wood, Habler, Al-Kahfah (2026) Large Empirical Case Study: Go-Explore adapted for AI Red Team Testing
finding: Go-Explore on a GPT-4o-mini tool agent: random seed variance was larger than the effect of algorithm settings. Single-seed comparisons are unreliable.
numbers: 5 seeds: 0 to 16 findings per configuration (8x spread). Tools-only signature 1.8 +/- 1.3 findings per seed; full-intent signature 4.6 +/- 6.0. Seed 42 gave 16 against a 5-seed mean of 4.6. Cumulative mean stabilized after 3-4 seeds in this setup. 28 runs, 6 research questions.
limits: Preprint, not shown to be peer reviewed. 90 s budget, one model. The authors warn the 3-4 seed rule comes from one ordering with no confidence intervals. 70-90% of findings were false positives.
agent_relevance: Our own bench must use several seeds before concluding anything about an archive arm; one lucky run misleads.

source: Bhatt et al. (2026) Go-Explore adapted for AI Red Team Testing, state signature and reward shaping
finding: State-key collapse: when the model refuses, 96% of attack intents mapped to one archive cell under the usual tool-based hash. Adding message intent to the hash separated them, yet the simple tools-only signature still found the verified attacks. Reward shaping on top hurt.
numbers: Reward bonus plus granular signatures: exploration fell 94% (161 findings). Reward bonus alone: 18 false positives, 0 verified attacks. All three enhancements together: zero findings. Ensemble of simple agents found 2 attacks of 2 types; the enhanced single agent found 5 attacks of 1 type. 13 verified attacks in total.
limits: Very low counts of verified attacks (1 to 5 per arm). Preprint. One environment. The reward-shaping collapse explanation is the authors' own and not isolated.
agent_relevance: Two warnings: check that the state key does not collapse different states into one cell, and do not add heuristic bonuses to node scores without a test.

source: Bhatt et al. (2026) Go-Explore adapted for AI Red Team Testing, ensemble scaling
finding: Many independent short runs with different seeds add diversity: without a guardrail attack types saturated near 20 agents (4 types) while attack count kept growing; with a guardrail diversity fell to 1 type.
numbers: Attack count reached 1054 at N=100 without guardrails. Each agent had 60 s. Diversity saturates near N=20 (4 types).
limits: Counts are findings, many unverified. Seeds, not algorithms, drive diversity. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Several short independent archives give breadth; one long archive gives depth. This maps to restarts versus deeper expansion (see the anytime search and restarts subfield).

source: Ecoffet et al. (2021) First return, then explore, robustification and evaluation standard
finding: Valid scores come only after robustification under sticky actions; raw archive trajectories are not robust. The authors flag that earlier Pitfall scores obtained without sticky actions are not comparable.
numbers: Robustification ran 10B frames on all Atari games except Solaris (20B) and Pitfall with domain knowledge (15B). The state-of-the-art table pools 23 algorithms and variants.
limits: Compute is very large. Equal-compute comparison against Agent57 or NGU not reported.
agent_relevance: 'Solve first, then make robust' has a counterpart in our schema: find a candidate with the archive, then re-verify it independently.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore, limitations
finding: Stated limits of the LLM archive loop: each new state is compared with the whole archive, which will not scale; the LLM may be biased about what counts as interesting; testing is mostly on games and one math puzzle.
numbers: Malformed LLM outputs under 0.1% of actions, with a random-choice failsafe.
quote: if a foundation model was biased to think that nothing 'purple' is interesting, we wouldn't explore states that are 'purple'
limits: Bias risk is argued, not measured. No tests on open real-world tasks such as coding.
agent_relevance: The 'interesting' judgement is a model-judged step with correlated-error risk. Back it with counts or code checks where possible.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Darwin Godel Machine, safety note
finding: The archive-driven self-improvement loop comes with a listed hallucination case study (appendix H) and was run with sandboxing and monitoring; the authors treat it as a safety problem needing oversight.
numbers: No numbers read; only the table of contents heading and the safety statement.
limits: I read the ablation tables and discussion, but the appendix case study only by heading. Flagged, not measured.
agent_relevance: A stronger searcher over a self-reported score may find ways to fake it. Scores that decide archive membership should come from checks outside the model.
